title: Strength gone, in chains
hook: strength is gone, I'm in chains, nothing works; Nanak says, only You are my refuge (Salok M9 53, ang 1429)

segments.voice: Yesterday: janjaal, and your line: today or tomorrow. Everything passes, so sing. Today the saloks turn from the world to one person, at the end of their strength.

The calls have been made, the forms filled out, the advice taken, and the problem is still sitting there. A diagnosis. A job search in its ninth month. A child who won't talk to you. Everything known has been tried, and at some point a person hears themselves say, out loud or not: I've got nothing left. It's a strange, bare place. Pride doesn't work there; cleverness doesn't either. Guru Tegh Bahadur has a salok from exactly that place, and Sikh tradition hears it as the words of a man in a cell.
screen: `EVERYTHING TRIED.` → `I'VE GOT NOTHING LEFT.` → `A SALOK FROM THAT PLACE.`

segments.voice: Salok fifty-three, Ang fourteen twenty-nine. In paraphrase: my strength is exhausted, I am bound in chains, and nothing I try works. Nanak says, now You are my shelter, Lord: help me, as You helped the elephant. Three phrases do the work. Bal chhutkio: strength has slipped away. Bandhan pare: the bonds have fallen on me. Kachhoo na hot upaai: no remedy, no plan, nothing works. It's an honest inventory, with nothing dressed up. Then the turn: ab ot. Now, the shelter. Ot means a refuge, a support, the wall you put your back against. And the salok adds an old picture, gaj, the elephant. Indian tradition tells of an elephant king seized by a crocodile in a lake. He pulled for a long time with all his great strength and lost. Only when he gave up pulling and called on God was he freed. Gurbani recalls this story as a sign of grace for the helpless. Why does this salok weigh so much for Sikhs? Tradition places it in the Guru's last months, when he was imprisoned in Delhi before his execution, and Sikhs hear it as written in real chains. Historians don't know exactly when each salok was composed, so that link is tradition. Either way, the shape is the point. The salok doesn't pretend strength is limitless. It admits the end of strength, and from there it asks. In Sikh thought, that asking isn't failure. It's where the ot, the shelter, finally gets leaned on.
screen: `BAL CHHUTKIO: STRENGTH HAS SLIPPED AWAY.` · `NOTHING WORKS: AN HONEST LIST.` · `OT: THE SHELTER YOU LEAN ON.` · `THE ELEPHANT WHO STOPPED PULLING.` · then, large: `ONLY YOU.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place where you've tried everything you know, and say it as plainly as the salok does: this is what I've tried; this is what isn't working. Then let yourself lean back, the way you'd lean against a wall. If you pray, ask God for help in your own words, or say Waheguru; if you don't, think of one person you could ask, and picture asking them.
Strength gone. Bal chhutkio, bandhan pare: strength slipped away, the bonds fell on me, and from there, the ot, the shelter.
Your line: only you. At the end of strength, asking isn't failure. Day six hundred four.

howItsDone: Sikhs read salok fifty-three as part of the closing saloks of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and many turn to it in illness or trouble as a plain cry for the Lord's shelter.

fork.setup: you're the elephant, seized by the crocodile, and your strength is running out. what does the story say freed you?
options: giving up the pulling and calling on God.
waiting for the crocodile to tire.
fork.reveal: in the story, strength lost. calling on God is what freed him, and the salok asks: help me, as You helped the elephant.

original.note: Gurmukhi: ot, a shelter or support; salok fifty-three turns on ab ot, now the shelter.

trapdoor: what you thought: strength gone is a line about weakness.
what it means: it's the honest end of self-reliance, and the moment of asking.
what a scholar hears: the gaj image recalls the Puranic story of the elephant king and the crocodile; tradition, not a dated record, ties the salok to the Guru's imprisonment in Delhi.
guess: an honest cry at the very end of one's strength
a curse asking that enemies lose their power
a hymn praising an elephant's great strength

chat.says: I've tried everything and nothing works. What does that salok about chains say?
options: It names that place honestly, then leans on the shelter and asks for help.
It says if nothing works, you just haven't tried hard enough yet.
It says asking for help is weakness, so keep pulling on your own.
chat.meaning: Bal chhutkio, bandhan pare: strength gone, bonds fallen. Then ab ot, now the shelter. In Sikh thought, that asking isn't failure.

ot.meaning: a refuge, a support, a wall to lean on

gaj.meaning: the elephant, freed when he called on God
